data.title: A small studio that draws for the people who will use the building.
data.intro: ARCA is a six-person architecture studio working on houses, small public buildings, interiors and gardens. This page describes how we work and who does what.

children.text: We keep the studio small on purpose. Marta draws the first sketches of every project and stays involved until the building is handed over, so the person you meet at the first site visit is the person who signs off the drawings.
How we work

Most of our work is one building at a time, for people who will live in it or run it. We start with a site visit and a written brief, build a physical model before the drawings are finished, and we visit the site often while it is being built.
We work in a handful of countries around the coast and in the mountains. Travel is part of the fee and is written down in the proposal, so there are no surprises.
What we do not do

We do not take on more projects than six people can follow properly. We do not promise a finish date before we have seen the site, the rules and the builder's programme. We do not use the photographs on this site as a promise of what your building will look like.
The people
The team is listed below with first names and roles. If you want to speak to one of us about a particular kind of project, the enquiry form lets you choose the type.

data.title: We design around the site, then check every step with you.
data.intro: Four phases, each with a written summary at the end. You can stop or change direction after any of them.

children.text: Sustainability, in plain terms
We do not hold or advertise a green certification. What we do on every project is simple and checkable, and we put it in the drawings so you and the builder can see it.
Sun and wind first

We set the building on the plot so that rooms get winter sun and summer shade, and so that most rooms have windows on two sides. Roof overhangs are sized from the sun angle on the plot, not copied from another job.
Heavy walls where days are hot
In hot, dry places we use thick masonry or concrete walls that hold the night's cool into the afternoon. In cold places we put the insulation outside the structure and keep the timber dry.
Materials from nearby

We ask local builders and quarries what they can supply before we choose finishes, and we prefer stone, lime and timber that can be repaired rather than replaced. We list what each material is and where it comes from.
Water and planting
Gardens are planted with species already growing on the site or nearby. Rainwater from roofs is directed to planting beds or a tank where the rules allow it.
What you get at each phase

After the site visit you get the one-page brief. After the concept phase you get the model and a short note comparing the layouts. After detailed design you get the drawings, the materials list and a cost check. At handover you get a care guide for the building.

data.title: How we charge, and what an enquiry means.
data.intro: A short, plain note on how the studio prices work.

children.text: We agree a fixed fee in writing for each phase before it starts. If the brief changes, we tell you what that does to the fee before we go on.
Before a fee is agreed
The first conversation and the first site visit within the studio's home region are free. A visit that needs a flight or an overnight stay is charged at cost, and we say so first.
What an enquiry is

Sending the enquiry form opens an email to the studio. It is not a booking and it does not commit either side to anything. We reply within three working days and may ask a few questions about the site.
Budget ranges
The budget range on the form is optional. It helps us say early whether the project is the right size for a studio of our size. We will not hold it against you if you leave it blank.

data.title: Cliff House
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Project architect: S. A.
Interiors: L. K.
Structure: Ferro & Dane Engineers
data.summary: A family house on a rock ledge, one room deep so every room looks at the sea.
data.description: The plot is a narrow ledge with a drop on one side and a road cut on the other. We put the house along the ledge, one room deep, with a rough stone wall facing the road and a long glass front facing the water. Each bedroom has a window on both sides, so the house cools itself with a cross breeze in summer. The deck is poured concrete, brushed by hand, and it keeps its shade under the roof edge until late afternoon.

data.title: Olive Court
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Project architect: D. P.
Landscape: T. V.
Local builder: Kritos Construction
data.summary: A small arts hall built around a single olive tree that was already on the site.
data.description: The village asked for a hall for classes, small concerts and market days. The only fixed point on the site was an old olive tree, so we kept it and built the hall around it. Three concrete walls wrap a courtyard, a shallow pool sits at the foot of the tree, and the hall opens onto the courtyard through full-height sliding glass. In summer the doors stay open and the courtyard works as a foyer.

gallery.caption: Afternoon shadows on the courtyard wall.

data.title: Forest Retreat
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Project architect: J. H.
Timber frame: Nordvik Trebygg
data.summary: Four guest rooms in a timber and concrete lodge set low among spruce trees.
data.description: The lodge sits on a shelf of ground between two stands of spruce. A concrete base holds the plan level and keeps the timber off the damp ground. Above it, a larch-clad volume holds four guest rooms and a shared room with a long window to the valley. We kept the footprint small so that no mature trees had to be cut, and every room has a view of the mountain.

gallery.caption: Larch slats against board-marked concrete at the entrance.

data.title: Terrace House
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Project architect: S. A.
Model maker: B. N.
data.summary: A house under one long concrete roof, with a lap pool that follows the edge of the hill.
data.description: A deep concrete roof shades the living room and a wide terrace, and slim steel posts carry it so the glass can stay clear of structure. The pool runs along the cliff edge and acts as a cooling surface beside the terrace. The house is under construction. The photographs show the design as drawn and modelled.

Section through the pool, 1:50

gallery.caption: The pool edge and terrace, as designed.

data.title: Lake Pavilion
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Concept design: D. P., B. N.
data.summary: A concept for a small lakeside hotel pavilion with a cantilevered upper floor.
data.description: A concept study for a family-run hotel on a lake shore. The upper floor of guest rooms cantilevers over a glazed lounge, and a water garden of boulders and reeds sits between the building and the lake. It is a design study only and has no site or client yet.

gallery.caption: A study of shadow on a board-marked concrete wall.

data.title: Stone Room
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Interiors: L. K.
Stone work: Piedra Viva workshop
data.summary: The interior of a seaside living room finished in limestone, oak and lime plaster.
data.description: An existing living room with a low ceiling and one large opening to the water. We lowered nothing and added nothing to the structure. Instead we limited the finishes to three materials, honed limestone on the floor, oak joinery and lime plaster on the walls, so the view stays the main thing in the room.

gallery.caption: The three finishes laid out on site.
A stone bowl made for the entrance table by a local mason.

data.title: Quarry Garden
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Landscape: T. V.
Model maker: B. N.
data.summary: A garden terraced into a disused limestone quarry, planted with what already grows there.
data.description: A concept for a guest garden in a former quarry. The cut faces stay as they are and become the garden walls. Terraces step down to a small house and a pool, and planting is limited to olives, rosemary and other species already growing on the hillside. The site area is approximate.

data.title: Harbour Hall
data.team:
Principal: M. R.
Project architect: D. P.
Structure: Ferro & Dane Engineers
data.summary: A community hall and market courtyard behind the old fish quay.
data.description: The town wanted a covered place for markets and meetings that stays usable in the heat. We drew a hall with deep walls and a courtyard planted with olive trees, with steps that double as seating. The building is under construction and is due to open next year.

gallery.caption: A trial panel for the wall finish, in afternoon sun.

data.title: Harbour Hall: first floor slab poured
data.summary: The first floor slab went in over two days. Next is the courtyard wall, where we are testing three finishes on a trial panel.

data.title: Visit the site
data.text: We walk the plot at different times of day, check access and services, and note the sun, wind and views. You tell us how you live, and we write a one-page brief for you to correct.

data.title: Concept and model
data.text: Two or three layouts as sketches, then one developed as a physical model. We bring the model to you rather than send images, because scale is easier to judge by hand.

data.title: Detailed design
data.text: Drawings for the planning authority and the builder, a materials list with samples, and a cost check against the budget. Changes are cheap on paper, so we expect a few.

data.title: Build and handover
data.text: We visit the site regularly, answer the builder's questions and check the work against the drawings. At handover you get a short guide to how the building is meant to be looked after.
